On a floor, a bin of work carries a card. It says what to make, how many, and which way.
Every station the bin passes reads the card, and writes down beside its own step how many good it made.
The card never counts itself done. At the end, somebody signs it off. That card is a work order.
Four words. An order says make this many of that material, this way. This way is its routing, the road from the last class.
Release means the order may now go to the floor. Until then it is a plan, and no machine works on it.
Dispatch is each machine's queue: the work it has next, in order. And finish is a person saying a step is done, and then the order.
This is the Orders page. Every order on the plant, its status, what was ordered and what has been booked.
A planner makes a new one. New order: a code, the material, and how many.
Forks, UT-FORK. Eleven thousand: about one shift of the fork line, at some twenty-three forks a minute.
We leave release unticked, so the order is only planned for now. Create.
Planned. Its steps were copied from the fork line's routing: Mold, Degate, Mark, each on its machine.
Now release it to the floor.
Released. Nothing has been made against it yet. Where does it show up? At the first machine of its road.
The station screen of the fork mould, FORK1_Mold. Its queue: the order it is running now, and ours behind it, nothing made yet.
That is dispatch. The operator does not hunt for paper: the machine's screen says what is next.
Each line of the queue says how many good of how many ordered. The next machine, the degating press, gets our order the same way.
The order in front of ours, WO-FORK1-0001, for 2,778 forks, released when the plant started. It is running.
Each step books what its own machine counted. Mold has made the most, then Degate, then Mark, the last.
The order's booked count is the last step's, not the sum. A fork moulded but not yet marked is not a finished fork.
Now what it refuses. The order has booked past its 2,778, the over-run says by how many, and it is still running.
An order does not finish itself when the count is reached. A line that has made its number is often still running.
So every fork it makes past the number is booked to this order, and the over-run is the true one. A person closes it.
Here that person finishes each step. Mold first.
Mold is done. The mould's next fork books to the order behind it in its queue, ours.
Degate, then Mark. Completed.
And the news goes up. In the outbox, a confirmation for the office, among the machines' state changes: WO-FORK1-0001, waiting to be sent.
It was written when a person finished the order, not when the count passed the number. So the office hears the number the line really made.
Back on the order: completed. The over-run beside the ordered number is every fork made past 2,778, still on the order that made them.
That is a work order's day: planned, released, dispatched, counted step by step, and finished by a person. You now know how to do three things.
